newsitem.title: USA: Dow tumbles, dollar up as bond rates soar on Fed worries.
newsitem.headline: Dow tumbles, dollar up as bond rates soar on Fed worries.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks tumbled and the dollar rose on Thursday, as long-term bond interest rates approached 7 percent after upbeat U.S. economic data revived fears of a rate hike by the Federal Reserve.

The Dow index fell 160.48 points to close at 6,878.89 --the fifth steepest fall in point terms in the history of the average. The decline of 2.28 percent, however, ranks nowhere near the top percentage losses.
Broader indexes were also sharply lower, with losers trouncing gainers 2,070 to 510 on heavy volume of 503.7 million on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts cited a stiff bond market sell-off as the primary catalyst for stocks' decline. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury fell nearly a full point, or 31 cents on a $1,000 bond, to drive the yield up to 6.96 percent, its highest level in nearly six months, from Wednesday's close of 6.88 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The Fed's interest rate policy meeting March 25 has been a major concern that has weighed on financial markets recently. On Thursday, however, investors no longer seemed uncertain about the meeting's outcome, analysts said.
"The market, in both bonds and stocks, is telling us a rate rise is a foregone conclusion," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.

Until Thursday, blue-chip stocks had continued their rise with only momentary lapses despite a steady rise in long-term bond interest rates. Now with rates near 7 percent, however, analysts said the rally suddenly appeared suspect.

"We really haven't seen much reason for improvement and yet stock prices have gone up," said Melissa Brown, director of quantitative research at Prudential Securities. "When stocks are overvalued and rates go up, that tends to magnify the issue."
Financial and transportation issues were hard hit, as both are particularly sensitive to interest rate changes.
The session's heaviest selling was reserved for a group with problems all their own: the tobacco stocks.
News that the Mississippi Supreme Court rejected a challenge to the state's Medicaid suit against tobacco companies sent tobacco stocks skidding.
Late on Thursday, the dollar fetched 123.34 Japanese yen, up from 122.27 yen late on Wednesday. The dollar climbed to 1.7047 German marks from 1.6928 marks.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices rose on indications that imports from Europe would slow.
April crude oil ended at $20.70 a barrel, up 8 cents.

A cold snap expected to hit the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market, boosted prices. April heating oil ended 0.14 cent per gallon higher at 54.22 cents, while April gasoline closed 0.40 cent per gallon lower at 64.23 cents.
On New York's Commodity Exchange, April gold closed up $1.30 an ounce at $354.40.
Overseas, London's benchmark FTSE 100 share index closed 24.8 points lower at 4,397.7. In Tokyo, the Nikkei average of 225 shares shed 282.79 points, or 1.56 percent, to end at 17,900.48.
